questions.name: AI Use-Case & Business Readiness

section_animation.0-0.9: arrow completely misses the target, the knight cries
section_animation.1-2.9: arrow hits the target, but not the bullseye
section_animation.3-4: arrow hits the bullseye and the knight celebrates

questions.description: Are you solving the right problems with AI?

questions.text: Q1. Is AI a strategic priority in your business today?

options.text: AI is not on our agenda yet
AI is discussed, but not prioritized
AI is included in strategy, but loosely defined
AI has a defined roadmap with clear business goals
AI is a core pillar with executive sponsorship

questions.text: Q2. How clearly are your AI use cases tied to business outcomes?

options.text: No defined AI use cases
Ideas exist, but not linked to measurable outcomes
Some use cases linked to efficiency or cost savings
Clear use cases tied to revenue, productivity, or risk
Use cases are prioritized, measured, and reviewed regularly

questions.text: Q3. Do you have an accountable owner for AI initiatives?

options.text: No clear owner
Responsibility is shared informally across teams
A sponsor exists, but AI is not their primary focus
A dedicated product owner or AI lead is accountable
Clear ownership with decision rights and budget authority

questions.text: Q4. How AI-ready are your core processes and data today?

options.text: Data is fragmented and mostly manual
Some data is digitized, but inconsistent
Key processes are standardized, data is usable
Data is clean, structured, and regularly used for decisions
Processes are designed with AI automation in mind

questions.text: Q5. Where are you in your AI experimentation journey?

options.text: No AI experimentation yet
Isolated experiments or proofs of concept
Pilots running in selected teams
AI solutions live in production
AI solutions are scaling across the organization

questions.name: AI Talent & Capability Readiness

section_animation.0-0.9: knight hurts hand when punching the bag
section_animation.3-4: knight punches bag and the bag bursts

questions.description: Do you have the people to make AI real?

questions.text: Q1. How clearly are AI-related roles defined in your organization?

options.text: No AI-related roles defined
Roles exist but responsibilities are unclear
Some AI roles defined, coverage is incomplete
Clear AI roles with defined responsibilities
AI roles mapped across delivery, governance, and scale

questions.text: Q2. How long does it typically take to fill advanced AI or data roles?

options.text: 6+ months
4–5 months
2–3 months
Within 2 months
We proactively build talent before demand peaks

questions.text: Q3. How confident are you in assessing AI talent during interviews?

options.text: Not confident at all
Some confidence, but largely intuition-based
Confident in technical skills, less so in application
Confident in both skills and real-world use cases
We use structured assessments and project-based evaluation

questions.text: Q4. How do you currently build AI capabilities internally?

options.text: No AI upskilling initiatives
Ad hoc courses or self-learning only
Some structured training, limited application
Structured upskilling with real project exposure
Continuous upskilling with mentoring and deployment

questions.text: Q5. Which best describes your AI talent strategy today?

options.text: Hire externally whenever there is a need
Primarily hire, limited internal development
Mix of hiring and internal upskilling
Deliberate build–buy–deploy strategy
Capability-first model aligned to business roadmap

questions.name: AI Execution, Adoption & Sustainability

section_animation.0-0.9: wooden sword breaks on training dummy and the knight cries
section_animation.1-2.9: wooden sword is wielded with some skill but is sweating profusely and struggling
section_animation.3-4: wooden sword is wielded with mastery, the dummy breaks and knight celebrates

questions.description: Can you move from Pilot to Production to Scale?

questions.text: Q1. How well do teams understand how AI affects their daily work?

options.text: Teams are unaware of AI implications
Awareness exists, but understanding is low
Some teams understand and apply AI tools
Clear role-level understanding across teams
AI is embedded into workflows and decision-making

questions.text: Q2. How mature is your AI governance (ethics, data, risk)?

options.text: No governance in place
Informal guidelines, inconsistently applied
Basic policies exist, limited enforcement
Defined governance framework with accountability
Governance embedded into delivery and review cycles

questions.text: Q3. How do you support continuous AI learning?

options.text: No structured learning support
External courses only, optional
Mix of external training and internal sharing
Structured learning with mentoring and practice
Continuous learning embedded into performance and roles

questions.text: Q4. What typically happens after an AI pilot?

options.text: Pilot stops after demo
Pilot is revisited slowly or inconsistently
Some pilots move to limited production
Clear path from pilot to production
Repeatable model to scale successful pilots

questions.text: Q5. How confident are you in sustaining AI initiatives beyond 12 months?

options.text: Not confident at all
Some confidence, high dependency on individuals
Moderately confident, risks remain
Confident with systems and talent in place
Very confident, AI is self-sustaining and scalable

knight_end_animation.high_average: knight's armor is really flashy, like gold and silver and celebrates in victory
knight_end_animation.average: knight's armor is normal, normal metals, stands with sword at side, nods in acknowledgment
knight_end_animation.low_average: knight is still in training clothes, but with a determined look
